Hawaii bans non-compete and non-solicit clauses between high-tech companies and their employees

While I have quit jobs over these types of issues, I believe it's the employer's right to use these.

You should be able to hire whom you want, fire whom you want, and do business with whom you want.

But I have other crazy beliefs, too. Like if a foreign company wants to do business in the US, their internal practices must at least match what US law requires. For example, the foreign company would have to pay its workers the same minimum wage that the US federal law mandates. Same would go for health and safety requirements.

What's the reasoning for this? Well, if we thought these things were important enough for our citizens to put them into law, why isn't it important enough for our trade partners?

I also think we should have something like a flat sales tax. 1% for the 1%, that way FedGov can't get up to too much mischief. US tax rates are ridiculous when you consider, back in the day when it was running the world, the Catholic Church only required a tithe (10%).

Not sure what any of those have to do with no-compete clauses. Those are restrictions that employers place on employees; they are effectively prior restraint on an employee's actions when they leave the employer. Just as employers should be able to hire whom they want, fire whom they want, and do business with whom they want, employees should be able to do the same.
Exactly! It's a contract that both have to willingly agree to enter.
The employees do when they sign it

On paper, sure. In real life, employers have way more leverage over employees than the other way round, and clauses like this that place prior restraint on a worker's employment after they leave are grossly unfair. It effectively prevents the employee from participating in the job market without making major changes to their life, and allows the employer to abuse this by not paying the employee competitive wages and benefits.

Oh, I know the consequences, and like I said, I have left jobs when they tried to institute non-compete, non-disclosure, and intellectual property agreements.

My point is that I don't believe the governent has any business saying what can and can't be in a contract that is willingly entered. They should only get involved once there's a breach that can't be settled amicably.

Employees are always free to form their own company and institute whatever policies they like.

Would this cause employers to be less likely to provide training to their employees? Get hired by company A, work there for a year while taking tons of classes. Then send your much improved resume to company B (who doesn't provide training) and get a presumably better paying job. Company A has to eat the cost of paying an employee to get trained along with the cost of training.

I know there are safeguards for a company paying for tuition and other external classed, but what about classes that the company provides internally?

This is a debatable point that I feel only time will tell, as there are several factors that come into play.

There's a quote out there with "What if we train them and they leave?" "What if we don't, and they stay?" Companies will always offer some degree of training, but core competencies are what get people hired. And you should never leave yourself in a position where only 1 person is trained on something. They can (and have) left on a moment's notice for reasons other than a career at a comparable company.

In the long run, employers are going to have to compete harder to attract the best people. Some may offer more training, others may find it more economical to offer vacation days. If training was the only currency in the corporate world, then yes, they would likely lower their training for some, while offering more for people in exchange for longer contracts. I am a serious Libertarian and I see no issues with banning non-compete clauses as they are typically written today. The only kind of contract I believe should be enforceable includes consideration. It should be like this for employees of any field. Just the premise of controlling what someone can or can't do when the company is no longer employing them is so scummy. I understand a company being afforded protections while the person is employed with them but beyond that it's silly.

I'm better when I eat more than the generaly-recommended amount of salt. We're probably on the same page here.

There's a condition called Orthostatic Intolerance that is associated with uncomfortably low blood pressure when standing, or even sitting upright. Increasing the amount of salt (or other electrolytes) in the diet tends to boost blood volume, and helps minimize the symptoms.

OI is often associated with CFS, and many us either have it to one degree or another, or suffer from something that seems similar.

Magnesium sulfate is another electrolyte which is sometimes used to alleviate CFS symptoms. I don't know if this is found in Gatorade or not, but it's another thing to consider. FWIW this particular substance has not had any effect on me.
